children: Google has found an interesting way to combat the sky-high energy costs involved in data centers-build them in an extremely cold country.

The tech giant announced a 13 billion-euro ($15 billion) investment in artificial-intelligence infrastructure in Finland, in a blog post Wednesday. It's one of Europe's coldest countries, with average winter temperatures in some regions falling as low as minus 20C, or minus 4F, according to local tourism organization Visit Finland.
The colder climate should reduce the costs of cooling down overheating servers.

Alphabet, like other megacap tech names Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Amazon, is spending big on AI. The company leads the way among its peers, though, committing to long-term spending of $811 billion for technical infrastructure and inventory as well as energy contracts and content licenses, Barron's recently reported. A quarter of that will be spent in the next 12 months.
Its Finland partnership won't put too much of a dent in those costs but every little helps.

Google has a 15-year history in the Nordic country, which began when it converted an old paper mill in the town of Hamina into a data center in 2009. Google uses cold seawater from the Bay of Finland for its cooling system at the site.

The latest announcement, Google's biggest single investment in Europe, includes digital infrastructure as well as clean energy projects. The company has signed a 22-year agreement to support a nuclear power plant in the country, add onshore wind capacity and fund a new battery system "to stabilize prices during cold, windless periods."
The stock was pointing 0.4% lower ahead of the open, and is up 8% so far this year.
